title: On the Wasserstein Geodesic Principal Component Analysis of probability measures
claim: A geodesic in the quotient space lifts to a horizontal geodesic in the total space, so computations can move to the lifted space.
layout: 2 stacked layers, top-to-bottom, projection arrow, red geodesics, dash-dot fibers
description: A line-drawn geometric sketch of two stacked curved surfaces. The large upper patch is labeled GL_d, the space of invertible matrices. The thin lower strip is labeled S_d^{++}, the space of covariance matrices. Three dash-dot curves run vertically through the upper patch. They are green fibers labeled π^{-1}(Id), π^{-1}(Σ1) and π^{-1}(Σ2), and each one continues down to a point in the lower strip (Id, Σ1, Σ2). A thick black arrow labeled π points downward between the two layers. In the upper patch a red segment from A1 to A2 is labeled 'horizontal geodesic', with a tangent vector X ∈ Hor_{A1}. In the lower strip a matching red segment from Σ1 to Σ2 is labeled 'Wasserstein geodesic'. Red text draws the eye first.
caption: The Bures-Wasserstein geometry of centered Gaussian distributions, inspired by [ref].
abstract: This paper focuses on Geodesic Principal Component Analysis (GPCA) on a collection of probability distributions using the Otto-Wasserstein geometry. The goal is to identify geodesic curves in the space of probability measures that best capture the modes of variation of the underlying dataset. We first address the case of a collection of Gaussian distributions, and show how to lift the computations in the space of invertible linear maps. For the more general setting of absolutely continuous probability measures, we leverage a novel approach to parameterizing geodesics in Wasserstein space with neural networks. Finally, we compare to classical tangent PCA through various examples and provide illustrations on real-world datasets.
